title: Bangladesh’s garment workers have a date for a pay rise. They still need a figure
subtitle: Factories in Ashulia closed again after a walkout. A new wage scale is due to take effect in December, but workers seeking 30,000 taka a month still do not know what they will take home.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Nasima Akter, a sewing-machine operator in Ashulia, Bangladesh, earns 14,500 taka a month. She told the Bangladeshi news service bdnews24.com that she could not afford to enrol her eldest daughter in college or pay the fee for her son’s secondary school examination form. When she joined the campaign for a higher garment wage, she already knew what her pay would have to cover.

On Thursday, 5 November, workers in Ashulia arrived for their shifts, then walked out and blocked a highway near Dhaka to demand a figure for the new minimum wage. More than 100 factories in the area suspended operations, the local industrial police superintendent told Reuters. A day earlier, worker and employer representatives had agreed on a date: the new scale would apply from 1 December, with the first payment in January. They had not agreed on an amount.

The protesters want a monthly minimum of 30,000 taka, up from 12,500. The current floor dates to November 2023, when it rose from 8,000 taka. It is the minimum, rather than every worker’s actual earnings, that the board must now determine. Akter already earns more than the floor; she told bdnews24.com that by payday much of her money was owed for rent and groceries.

Women make up most of the roughly four million people working in Bangladesh’s garment industry, according to the Associated Press. Not everyone who wants a pay rise took part in the walkout. Shilpi Khatun, a garment worker who did not join Thursday’s protest, told Reuters: “The prices of everything have gone up, but wages have not.”

The government formed a six-member board on 1 November. At its first meeting on 4 November, union representative Babul Akhter and employer representative A B M Shamsuddin both confirmed the timetable for paying December wages, Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha, the national news agency, reported. Board chair Syed Azad Subhani said he expected written proposals from both sides at the next meeting.

Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation, urged workers’ organisations to help draw up a pay proposal and workers to resume production while talks continued. He also called for the release of arrested workers and labour leaders. Representatives raised leave and trade union rights alongside pay. In Ashulia the following morning, workers who walked out were asking for more than an assurance that negotiations had begun.

Garments account for more than four-fifths of Bangladesh’s export earnings. Manufacturers say interruptions during the peak ordering season could delay shipments. They have also cited energy shortages, rising costs and competition from other producing countries in arguing that factories cannot afford to double the minimum wage.

International buyers have choices about how tightly those deadlines bind. After flooding disrupted Bangladeshi suppliers earlier this year, the Business and Human Rights Centre asked 15 major buyers how they had responded. The five that completed its questionnaire said they had allowed or would allow delivery delays without penalties. Primark said it had covered air-freight costs where necessary. Those answers concerned flooding; they are not commitments to pay suppliers more under a new wage scale.

For now, workers and manufacturers can plan around a date, but neither can calculate a payslip or the cost of an order from it. The next decision is the rate the board recommends. For families such as Akter’s, its value will be measured in what is left after rent and food, when a child brings home an examination form.
